Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072974/assets/a4de9d9df51efcec67253a1c7118466f29459ffd5c9136c144d33500ec5557bc.png)

The region $D$ is a type I region in the $yz$-plane:

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\sqrt{2y}-1\le z\le 2-\frac{y}{2}}.
$$

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y$ to $\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z,$ we split $D$ into two type II regions.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072974/assets/18bb3e55f076e022176bb60df27d5665ed2d91d75d618969c04ce192378db922.png)

Notice that the bottom and top boundaries of the lower region, written in the form $y=y(z),$ are

$\,$ $y=0\,$ and $\,y=\frac{1}{2}(z+1)^{2}.$

Also, the bottom and top boundaries of the upper region, written in the form $y=y(z),$ are

$\,$ $y=0\,$ and $\,y=4-2z.$

So, we can write $D$ as a union of

$$
{D}_{1}={(y,z)\,:\,-1\le z\le 1,\,0\le y\le \frac{1}{2}(z+1)^{2}}
$$

and

$$
{D}_{2}={(y,z)\,:\,1\le z\le 2,\,0\le x\le 4-2z}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{(z+1)^{2}/2}{\int }_{-2z}^{y+3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z+{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4-2z}{\int }_{-2z}^{y+3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

q-162414.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Plane Curve Given in Parametric Form
q-162414.source_problem:
The curvature of the plane curve $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+t\,j$ is given by 

$$
κ(t)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{},\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

 
What is the missing part of the expression?
q-162414.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =1 \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 0-(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 1|}{{((\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+{1}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|\operatorname{cos}⁡t|}{{({sin}^{2}⁡t+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\sqrt{{({sin}^{2}⁡t+1)}^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we removed the absolute value because cosine is positive for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$

q-162418.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Plane Curve Given in Parametric Form
q-162418.source_problem:
The signed curvature of the plane curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-{t}^{2}⟩$ is given by

$$
k(t)=\frac{2\cdot (\,\,)}{\sqrt{({cos}^{2}⁡t+4{t}^{2})^{3}}}.
$$

What is the missing part of the expression?
q-162418.worked_solution:
The signed curvature $k(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t)⟩$ is given by

$$
k(t)=\frac{{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y(t)=-{t}^{2}.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =-2t \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the signed curvature, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}k(t) & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-2)-(-2t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}{{((\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{{({cos}^{2}⁡t+4{t}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}{\sqrt{({cos}^{2}⁡t+4{t}^{2})^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

q-162517.knowledge_point: Determining a Stream Function for a Vector Field
q-162517.source_problem:
Which of the following is a stream function for the vector field
$F(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y\,i-2x{y}^{2}\,j?$
q-162517.worked_solution:
A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that $F(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y\,i-2x{y}^{2}\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=-2x{y}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=4xy+(-4xy)=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y,\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2}.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}=(xy)^{2}.
$$

q-16400.knowledge_point: Writing First-Order Linear ODEs in Standard Form
q-16400.source_problem:
Write the following first-order linear ODE in standard form.

$$
2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=1-4y\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$
q-16400.worked_solution:
A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Converting the given equation to standard form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =1-4y\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ 2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =1+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}y & ={{\frac{1+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the equation is written in standard form with $P(x)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $Q(x)=\frac{1+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}.$

q-16642.knowledge_point: Calculating the x-Intercepts of an Ellipse
q-16642.source_problem: Calculate the points where the ellipse $\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{9}=1$ intercepts the $x$-axis.
q-16642.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercept, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-3)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-3)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(0-2)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-3)^{2}}{4}+\frac{4}{9} & =1 \\ 9(x-3)^{2}+16 & =36 \\ 9(x-3)^{2} & =20 \\ (x-3)^{2} & =\frac{20}{9} \\ x-3 & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{20}{9}} \\ x & =3\pm \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at the points $(3-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3},0)$ and $(3+\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3},0).$

q-16645.knowledge_point: Calculating the x-Intercepts of an Ellipse
q-16645.source_problem: Calculate the points where the ellipse $\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{9}=1$ intercepts the $x$-axis.
q-16645.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercept, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(0-1)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{25}+\frac{1}{9} & =1 \\ 9(x+1)^{2}+25 & =9\cdot 25 \\ 9(x+1)^{2}+25 & =225 \\ 9(x+1)^{2} & =200 \\ (x+1)^{2} & =\frac{200}{9} \\ x+1 & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{200}{9}} \\ x & =-1\pm \frac{10\sqrt{2}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at the points $(-1-\frac{10\sqrt{2}}{3},0)$ and $(-1+\frac{10\sqrt{2}}{3},0).$

q-17392.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Sum Containing a Natural Logarithm Function
q-17392.source_problem: Given that $y=2{x}^{e}-ln⁡x$, find the instantaneous rate of change at $x=1.$
q-17392.worked_solution:
To find the instantaneous rate of change at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{e}-ln⁡x) \\  & =2e{x}^{e-1}-\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change at $x=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(2e{x}^{e-1}-\frac{1}{x})|}_{x=1} \\  & =2e\cdot {1}^{e-1}-\frac{1}{1} \\  & =2e-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-17544.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order ODE Using a Substitution
q-17544.source_problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{y+2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{x}
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{-1}.$*
q-17544.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-1}\,⟹\,y={z}^{-1}\,
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{z}^{-1}+2{x}^{2}{z}^{-2}}{x} \\ -\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{xz}+\frac{2x}{{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{z}{x}-2x\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{z}{x}-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z & =-2x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-2x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot (-2x) \\ x\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =-2{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz) & =-2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,\text{d}x & =-\int 2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ xz & =-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-2{x}^{3}}{3x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =\frac{C-2{x}^{3}}{3x} \\ y & =\frac{3x}{C-2{x}^{3}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-17559.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order Initial Value Problem Using a Substitution
q-17559.source_problem:
Solve the initial value problem 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{y(y-1)}{x}=0,\,y(1)=5,\,x>0.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z=\frac{1}{x}
$$

using the substitution $z={y}^{-1}.$*
q-17559.worked_solution:
The substitution $z={y}^{-1}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=\frac{1}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x>0.$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\ x\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,\text{d}x & =\int 1\,\text{d}x \\ xz & =x+C \\ z & =\frac{x+C}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =\frac{x+C}{x} \\ y & =\frac{x}{x+C}\end{aligned}
$$

We now determine $C$ from the initial condition  $y(1)=5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =\frac{1}{1+C}\,⟹\,C=-\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{(x-\frac{4}{5})} \\  & =\frac{5x}{(5x-4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-18688.knowledge_point: Solving a System Containing Decimals in One Equation
q-18688.source_problem:
Find the solution of the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}b=2a-1 \\ 1.5a+0.5b=2.5\end{aligned}
$$
q-18688.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the second equation by $10,$ as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}b=2a-1 &  \\ 1.5a+0.5b=2.5 & |\,\times 10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}b=2a-1 \\ 15a+5b=25\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the first equation is already solved for $b:$

$$
b=2a-1
$$

Now, to find the value of $a,$ we can substitute $b=2a-1$ into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}15a+5(2a-1) & =25 \\ 15a+10a-5 & =25 \\ 25a & =30 \\ a & =\frac{30}{25} \\ a & =1.2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $a=1.2$ into the  first equation to get:

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =2(1.2)-1 \\  & =2.4-1 \\  & =1.4\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $a=1.2$ and $b=1.4.$

q-19493.knowledge_point: Approximating the Value of a Function at a  Point Using Its Taylor Series
q-19493.source_problem: Use the first two non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of ${x}^{1/3}$ about $x=8$ to approximate the value of ${7}^{1/3}.$
q-19493.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=8.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{1/3} \\ f(8) & ={8}^{1/3}=2 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-2/3} \\ {f}^{′}(8) & =\frac{1}{3}(8)^{-2/3}=\frac{1}{3\cdot 4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{1/3} & =2+\frac{1}{3\cdot 4}(x-8)+⋯ \\  & =2+\frac{x-8}{12}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=7$ into the above to approximate ${7}^{1/3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{7}^{1/3} & ≈2+\frac{7-8}{12} \\  & =2-\frac{1}{12} \\  & =\frac{23}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-20362.knowledge_point: Finding the System of Equations Associated With an Augmented Matrix
q-20362.source_problem:
What would be the system of equations for the following augmented matrix?

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 3 & 2 \\ 4 & 3 & 4 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$
q-20362.worked_solution:
The augmented matrix consists of two parts: the coefficient matrix and the column of constants.

The coefficient matrix represents the coefficients in the linear system, while the column of constants represents the constants on the right-hand sides of the equations.

Using the variables $x$, $y$, and $z,$ then, the corresponding system of equations is

$$
{\begin{aligned}2x+y+2z=1 \\ 3x+2y+3z=2 \\ 4x+3y+4z=3.\end{aligned}
$$

q-20851.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Parametric Curve
q-20851.source_problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=2\sqrt{t},\,y=12t+1,\,0\le t<\infty ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=1.$
q-20851.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},\,{y}^{′}(t)=12.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{12}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}}=12\sqrt{t}.
$$

At the point where $t=1$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =12\sqrt{1} \\  & =12\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-20966.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Singular 3x3 System of Equations with One Pivot
q-20966.source_problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 4 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
q-20966.worked_solution:
The system corresponding to $M$ is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-y+4z=-1 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final two equations $0x+0y+0z=0,$ we can remove these equations from the system. So, our system now consists of just a single equation:

$$
x-y+4z=-1
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have two free variables $y$ and $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y,z.$ Doing this, we get

$$
x=-1+y-4z.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-1+y-4z \\ y=y \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$, $z$ (free variables) are arbitrary numbers.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1+y-4z \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+y[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+z[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

For the parametric curve (shown above)

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=1.$
q-20990.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

{x}^{′}(t)=2{e}^{t}(t+1),\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t+2.

At the point where $t=1$ we have

\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{e}\,.\end{aligned}

q-21353.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions
q-21353.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062586/assets/4aa2bca8faab077c47fb968882579233babe7d323ba3120088e8ea5599fbd570.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={e}^{t},\,y=t$
from $t=0$ to $t=2$ (shown above)?
q-21353.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{({e}^{t})^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+1}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-2194.knowledge_point: Integrating Functions Containing the Natural Logarithm
q-2194.worked_solution:
Let's set $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\sqrt{2}\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{ln}⁡x|+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-225023.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14046771/assets/33e48fa5bdbb034bcf489e038ccf80fc5f67baabeccacc1b7abd741183ebf05d.png)

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (x(u,v),y(u,v)),
$$

where 

$$
x=v(2-u),\,y=u{v}^{3}.
$$

The image of the side ${S}_{3}$ under the action of $T$ is given by

$$
x=x(t),\,y=t,\,1\ge t\ge 0.
$$

Find the function $x(t).$
q-225023.worked_solution:
To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the side ${S}_{3}.$

For the side ${S}_{3},$ we have $1\ge u\ge 0$ and $v=1.$ Substituting $v=1$ into our transformation equations, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(v(2-u),\,u{v}^{3}) \\  & =(1(2-u),\,u(1)^{3}) \\  & =(2-u,u).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the image of ${S}_{3}$ can be parametrized by

$$
x=2-u,\,y=u,\,1\ge u\ge 0.
$$

 

Writing this in the usual notation, we have

$$
x(t)=2-t,\,y(t)=t,\,1\ge t\ge 0.
$$

q-2939.knowledge_point: Calculating the Rate of Change of a Leg Using the Pythagorean Theorem
q-2939.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14066033/assets/9283bcc77ac8e63c1ba00f9a81e659bcbcf41bc98b94a1a0617b02feab71cf0a.png)

Car $B$ is being driven due south toward Caltech at a speed of $60\,\text{km/h},$ while car $A$ is being driven due east away from Caltech. When car $B$ is $0.6\,\text{km}$ away from Caltech, car $A$ is $0.8\,\text{km}$ from Caltech. If the distance between the two vehicles is increasing at a rate of $20\,\text{km/h},$ what is the speed of car $A?$
q-2939.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14066033/assets/6e7ef0d4665710a31c1c601048498f20ad6b3099769c1d140320074805964ec7.png)

In the diagram,

- $x$ is the distance between Caltech and car $A$,

- $y$ is the distance between Caltech and car $B$,

- $z$ is the distance between the two cars.

As shown in the diagram, $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ form a right triangle with $z$ as the hypotenuse. We wish to find the rate of change of $x,$ which is $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ 

We know that $x=0.8\,\text{km}$ and $y=0.6\,\text{km}.$ We can find $z$ using the Pythagorean Theorem, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ {0.8}^{2}+{0.6}^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ {z}^{2} & =1 \\ z & =1\,\text{km}\end{aligned}
$$

We also know that:

- $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=-60\,\text{km}/\text{h},$

- $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=20\,\text{km}/\text{h}.$

Finally, we differentiate both sides of ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={z}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ and then substitute in the known values, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({z}^{2}) \\ 2x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} \\ 2(0.8)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2(0.6)(-60) & =2(1)(20) \\ 1.6\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =40+72 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{112}{1.6} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =70.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the speed of the car $A$ is $70\,\text{km}/\text{h}.$

q-2941.knowledge_point: Calculating the Rate of Change of a Leg Using the Pythagorean Theorem
q-2941.source_problem:
A rocket that is launched vertically is tracked by a radar station located on
the ground $3\,\text{km}$ from the launch site. What is the vertical speed of the rocket at the instant when its distance from the radar station is $5\,\text{km}$ and this distance is increasing at a rate of $1\,000\,\text{km/h}?$
q-2941.worked_solution:
We start by drawing a diagram of the problem.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069977/assets/7af033f137fd76e5e3003926a598e695f4e0852b11dc27dfa84d58040144972b.png)

In the diagram,

- $x$ is the distance between the radar station and the launch point,

- $y$ is the distance between the launch point and the rocket, and

- $z$ is the distance between the radar station and the rocket.

As shown in the diagram, $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ form a right triangle with $z$ as the hypotenuse. We wish to find the rate of change of $y,$ which is $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.$ 

We know that $x=3\,\text{km}$ and $z=5\,\text{km}.$ We can find $y$ using the Pythagorean Theorem, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ {3}^{2}+{y}^{2} & ={5}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & =16 \\ y & =4\,\text{km}\end{aligned}
$$

We also know that:

- $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=1\,000\,\text{km}/\text{h},$

- the distance between the radar station and the launch point ($x$) remains the same, so $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=0.$

Finally, we differentiate both sides of ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={z}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ and then substitute in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({z}^{2}) \\ 2x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} \\ 2(3)(0)+2(4)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2(5)(1\,000) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{10\,000}{8} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =1\,250\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertical speed of the rocket is $1\,250\,\text{km}/\text{h}.$

q-30052.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation When the Solutions Are Rational
q-30052.source_problem: The equation ${x}^{2}-4x+4=9$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $\,p+q,$ and the sum of the roots ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}.$
q-30052.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+4 & =9 \\ {x}^{2}-4x & =5 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 2\cdot x & =5 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 2\cdot x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2} & =5 \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2\cdot x+{2}^{2})-4 & =5 \\ (x-2)^{2}-4 & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}-4 & =5 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=-2,q=9,$ and $p+q=7.$

Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2} & =9 \\ \sqrt{(x-2)^{2}} & =\sqrt{9} \\ x-2 & =\pm 3 \\ x & =2\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =2+3=5 \\ {x}_{2} & =2-3=-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are ${x}_{1}=-1$ and ${x}_{2}=5.$ Thus, the sum is $4.$

q-31872.knowledge_point: Determining the Row Operations Required To Find the Inverse of a 2x2 Matrix
q-31872.source_problem:
The inverse of the matrix $J$ is found using row operations, as shown below. What are the row operations corresponding to the blank spaces?

$$
\begin{aligned}[J\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{6} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
q-31872.worked_solution:
We write down $J$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $J$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[J\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{5}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+\frac{5}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{6} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding row operations are

$$
{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1},\,{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2},\,{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+\frac{5}{2}{R}_{2}.
$$

The matrix ${J}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{J}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{5}{6} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

q-31945.knowledge_point: Determining the Row Operations Required To Find the Inverse of a 2x2 Matrix
q-31945.source_problem:
The inverse of the matrix $K$ is found using row operations, as shown below. What are the row operations corresponding to the blank spaces?

$$
\begin{aligned}[K\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
q-31945.worked_solution:
We write down $K$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $K$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[K\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3} & -\frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{4}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding row operations are

$$
{R}_{1}:=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1},\,{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1},\,{R}_{2}:=3{R}_{2},\,{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{2}.
$$

The matrix ${K}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{K}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

q-31954.knowledge_point: Identifying the Inverse of a 2x2 Matrix Calculated Using Row Operations
q-31954.source_problem:
The inverse of the $2\times 2$ matrix $D$ is found using row operations, as shown below. Complete the process, and determine ${D}^{-1}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[D\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 &  &  \\ 0 & 1 &  & \end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
q-31954.worked_solution:
We write down $D$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $D$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[D\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix ${D}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{D}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

q-32247.knowledge_point: Solving a Consistent System of Equations Using Gauss-Jordan Elimination
q-32247.source_problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=4 \\ -2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
q-32247.worked_solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 4 \\ -2 & -3 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Using the standard Gauss-Jordan method, we can reduce this matrix to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 4 \\ -2 & -3 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 10 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The corresponding system is now  

$$
{\begin{aligned} & {x}_{1}+10{x}_{3}=-8 \\  & {x}_{2}-6{x}_{3}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ and we have one free variable, ${x}_{3}.$ That means we need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ in terms of ${x}_{3}.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=-8-10{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2}=6+6{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}={x}_{3},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{3}$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8-10{x}_{3} \\ 6+6{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-324453.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a Linear System of Differential Equations

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}

q-32546.knowledge_point: Finding the LU Factorization of a 2x2 Matrix
q-32546.source_problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}]$ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$
q-32546.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices: 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

q-32876.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve
q-32876.source_problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j+t\,k$ at the point $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2}),$ valid for real values of $u?$
q-32876.worked_solution:
The point $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point,  the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =-i+0\,j+\frac{3}{2}\,k \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j+t\,k & =-i+0\,j+\frac{3}{2}\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t=-1 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t=0 \\ t=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=\frac{3}{2}.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is at the tip of the vector $r(\frac{3}{2}).$  

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\frac{3}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{3}{2}) & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\,j+\,k \\  & =0\,i+\pi \,j+\,k \\  & =\pi \,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is

$$
R(u)=-i+\frac{3}{2}\,k+u\,(\pi \,j+\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

q-33203.knowledge_point: Finding the Intersection Point of a Line and a Plane Given in Other Forms
q-33203.source_problem:
Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:r=⟨-5,0,1⟩+t⟨-3,1,0⟩,\,Π:-3x+y-2z+27=0.
$$
q-33203.worked_solution:
Let's start by writing the equation of the line as

$$
r=⟨-5-3t,t,1⟩.
$$

Let's also write the equation of the plane in the dot product form:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+y-2z+27 & =0 \\ -3x+y-2z & =-27 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27 \\ r\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨-5-3t,t,1⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27 \\ ⟨-5-3t,t,1⟩\cdot ⟨-3,1,-2⟩ & =-27 \\ -3(-5-3t)+1\cdot t-2\cdot 1 & =-27 \\ 15+9t+t-2 & =-27 \\ 10t & =-40 \\ t & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=-4$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨-5-3(-4),-4,1⟩ \\  & =⟨7,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $P(7,-4,1).$

q-33205.knowledge_point: Finding the Intersection Point of a Line and a Plane Given in Other Forms
q-33205.source_problem:
Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:r=⟨-1,-2,6⟩+t⟨2,5,4⟩,\,Π:x+2y+z-33=0.
$$
q-33205.worked_solution:
Let's start by writing the equation of the line as

$$
r=⟨-1+2t,-2+5t,6+4t⟩.
$$

Let's also write the equation of the plane in the dot product form:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y+z-33 & =0 \\ x+2y+z & =33 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨1,2,1⟩ & =33 \\ r\cdot ⟨1,2,1⟩ & =33\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨-1+2t,-2+5t,6+4t⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨1,2,1⟩ & =33 \\ ⟨-1+2t,-2+5t,6+4t⟩\cdot ⟨1,2,1⟩ & =33 \\ -1+2t+2(-2+5t)+6+4t & =33 \\ -1+2t-4+10t+6+4t & =33 \\ 16t & =32 \\ t & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P,$ we substitute $t=2$ into the equation of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨-1+2(2),-2+5(2),6+4(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨3,8,14⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the intersection point is $P(3,8,14).$

q-333856.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Homogeneous System Using a Given Matrix Exponential
q-333856.source_problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$*
q-333856.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$

q-335312.knowledge_point: Constructing a Falling Body Model With Quadratic Drag
q-335312.source_problem:
A rock of mass $2\,\text{kg}$ falls vertically downward. Let $v(t)$ be the rock's velocity, in meters per second, $t\ge 0$ seconds after the fall began, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the rock is proportional to the square of the rock's velocity and acts in the direction opposite to motion.

Which differential equation best models the velocity? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, the acceleration due to gravity is $g,$ and the only forces acting on the rock are the weight due to gravity and drag.
q-335312.worked_solution:
Recall Newton's second law, which states that the resultant force $F$ acting on a body equals the product of its mass $m$ and acceleration $a:$

$$
F=ma
$$

In our case, two forces are acting on the rock:

- The force due to gravity, given by the weight $w$ of the rock, which equals

$$
\begin{aligned}w & =mg \\  & =2g.\end{aligned}
$$

- The force due to drag (air resistance) $D,$ which is proportional to the square of the velocity of the rock (and negative since it acts in the negative direction):

$$
D=-k{v}^{2},
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Note that, since drag, in $\text{N}=\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m/s}}^{2},$ is the product of the constant $k$ and squared velocity, in $(\text{m/s})^{2}={\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ the units of $k$ are

$$
\frac{\text{N}}{{\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{s}}^{2}}=\frac{\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m/s}}^{2}}{{\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{s}}^{2}}=\text{kg/m}.
$$

Summing the forces, the resultant force acting on the rock is

$$
F=w+D=2g-k{v}^{2}.
$$

Also, recall that acceleration is the derivative of velocity: $a=\frac{dv}{dt}.$
Substituting this into Newton's second law, along with our expression for the resultant force on the rock, we get

$$
2g-k{v}^{2}=2\,\frac{dv}{dt}\,⟹\,\frac{dv}{dt}=g-\frac{k}{2}{v}^{2}.
$$

q-3435.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation When the Solutions Are Irrational
q-3435.source_problem: The equation ${z}^{2}-50=-10z$ can be written in the form $(z+p{)}^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q,$ and solve the equation.
q-3435.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, the $-10z$ term to the left-hand side, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2}-50 & =-10z \\ {z}^{2}+10z & =50 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot 5\cdot z & =50 \\ {z}^{2}+2\cdot 5\cdot z+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2} & =50 \\ (z+5{)}^{2}-{5}^{2} & =50\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(z+5{)}^{2}-{5}^{2} & =50 \\ (z+5{)}^{2} & =75\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=5,q=75,$ and $p+q=80.$

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(z+5{)}^{2} & =75 \\ \sqrt{(z+5{)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{75} \\ |z+5| & =\sqrt{75} \\ z+5 & =\pm 5\sqrt{3} \\ z & =-5\pm 5\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

q-345274.knowledge_point: Determining the Indicial Equation of an ODE
q-345274.source_problem:
$$
-7{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+2x{y}^{′}+(x-5)y=0
$$

Find the indicial equation for a Frobenius series solution about the regular singular point $x=0$ of the differential equation above.
q-345274.worked_solution:
If $x=0$ is a regular singular point of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation, then the method of Frobenius states that there is at least one solution of the form

$$
y={x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n},
$$

where $\lambda $ and ${a}_{n}$ for $n=0,1,2,…$ are constants.

Substituting this solution and its derivatives into the ODE, collecting like terms, and setting coefficients equal to zero, we obtain: 

- the indicial equation from the coefficients of the $n=0$ term for arbitrary ${a}_{0},$ and

- a recurrence formula from the coefficients of the $n\ge 1$ terms.

**Step 1**: Write the solution $y$ as a Frobenius power series:

$$
y={x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n}={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the derivatives ${y}^{′}$ and ${y}^{″}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-1}, \\ {y}^{″} & ={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(\lambda +n-1)(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Rewrite all the series so that they use the same index of summation.

The terms of the differential equation are

$$
\begin{aligned}-7{x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =-7{x}^{2}\cdot {\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(\lambda +n-1)(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-2} \\  & =-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }7((\lambda +n)^{2}-(\lambda +n)){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}, \\ 2x{y}^{′} & =2x\cdot {\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n-1} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }2(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}, \\ (x-5)y & =(x-5){\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n+1}-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }5{a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the first sum of the $y$ term, we change the index of the summation by writing $m=n+1.$ This gives

$$
(x-5)y={\sum }_{m=1}^{\infty }{a}_{m-1}{x}^{\lambda +m}-{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }5{a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}.
$$

Then, replacing $m$ with $n$ (since it does not matter which letter we use) and isolating the $n=0$ term gives

$$
(x-5)y={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n-1}{x}^{\lambda +n}-5{a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }5{a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}.
$$

Similarly, isolating the $n=0$ terms for the other terms in the ODE, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-7{x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =-7({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }7((\lambda +n)^{2}-(\lambda +n)){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}, \\ 2x{y}^{′} & =2\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }2(\lambda +n){a}_{n}{x}^{\lambda +n}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Consolidate all the series into a single series that is equal to $0.$

Collecting the terms for $n=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-7({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda ){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+2\lambda {a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }-5{a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda } & = \\ (-7{\lambda }^{2}+7\lambda +2\lambda -5){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda } & = \\ (-7{\lambda }^{2}+9\lambda -5){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }. & \end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, collecting terms for $n\ge 1,$ we obtain an infinite series of the form
${x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(\lambda ){x}^{n},$
for some ${b}_{n}(\lambda ),$ $n\ge 1.$
Therefore, substituting into the homogeneous ODE, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(-7{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -5){a}_{0}{x}^{\lambda }+{x}^{\lambda }{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(\lambda ){x}^{n} & =0 \\ (-7{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -5){a}_{0}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(\lambda ){x}^{n} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5**:  Set the coefficients of the series equal to $0.$

Setting the coefficient of the $n=0$ term equal to $0$ with arbitrary ${a}_{0}\ne 0,$ we obtain the indicial equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-7{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -5){a}_{0} & =0 \\ 7{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-345668.knowledge_point: Determining the First Solution in the General Solution Using the Method of Frobenius
q-345668.source_problem:
Consider the following differential equation.

$$
16{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+(x-5)x{y}^{′}+(5+2x)y=0
$$

The general solution near $x=0$ of the differential equation is given by

$$
y={c}_{1}{y}_{1}(x)+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(x),
$$

where ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ are arbitrary constants and ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are linearly independent solutions. According to the Frobenius method, what is the best choice for the first solution ${y}_{1},$ where ${a}_{n}$ for $n=0,1,2,…$ are constants determined by substitution?

*Hint: You may assume $x=0$ is a regular singular point of the ODE and the indicial equation of the ODE is $16{\lambda }^{2}-21\lambda +5=0.$*
q-345668.worked_solution:
The general solution near a regular singular point $x=0$ of a second-order homogeneous linear differential equation with indicial roots ${\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}$ is given by

$$
y={c}_{1}{y}_{1}(x)+{c}_{2}{y}_{2}(x),
$$

where

- ${y}_{1}(x)={x}^{{\lambda }_{1}}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}({\lambda }_{1}){x}^{n}$ is the first Frobenius solution corresponding to the larger root of the indicial equation, and

- ${a}_{n}({\lambda }_{1})$ are the coefficients produced by the method when $\lambda ={\lambda }_{1}.$

We are given that the indicial equation is $16{\lambda }^{2}-21\lambda +5=0.$
Solving for the roots, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}16{\lambda }^{2}-21\lambda +5 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(16\lambda -5) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =\frac{5}{16},1\end{aligned}
$$

The larger solution is ${\lambda }_{1}=1.$ Therefore, the first Frobenius series solution we take is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={x}^{1}{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n}=x{\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{x}^{n}.
$$

q-36023.knowledge_point: Finding the Vector Equation of a Straight Line Given Parametrically

q-36696.knowledge_point: Computing Limits of Piecewise Functions with a Gap in the Domain
q-36696.source_problem:
Find ${lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}f(x)$ and ${lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{-}}f(x)$ for the function given by

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sec}⁡x & \text{ for }\,-\frac{\pi }{2}<x<0 \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡x & \text{ for }\,\frac{\pi }{2}<x<\pi \end{aligned}
$$
q-36696.worked_solution:
The right-sided limit ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x)$ does not exist since $f(x)$ is not defined on the interval $x\in (0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$ 

Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x)=\text{DNE}.
$$

Approaching $x=0$ from the left, we have $x<0,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=\operatorname{sec}⁡x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}\operatorname{sec}⁡x \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x)=\text{DNE},\,{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}f(x)=1.
$$

q-36754.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient
q-36754.source_problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}=1$ at the point $(0,0,2).$
q-36754.worked_solution:
First, note that we can write the equation of our surface as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,0,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,0,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1)k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+\frac{2y}{9}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{2}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,0,2) & =2(0)\text{ }i+\frac{2(0)}{9}\text{ }j+\frac{(2)}{2}\text{ }k \\  & =k \\  & =⟨0,0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, the vector form of the equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(0,0,2)$ and passes through the point $(0,0,2)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨0,\,0,\,2⟩+t\,∇f(0,0,2)=⟨0,\,0,\,2⟩+t\,⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

q-37774.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Singular 3x3 System of Equations with Two Pivots
q-37774.source_problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
q-37774.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $M$ is already in row echelon form. The system corresponding to $M$ is 

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+0y+3z=7 \\ 0x+y+2z=-3 \\ 0x+0y+0z=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final equation $0x+0y+0z=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of just two equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+3z=7 \\ y+2z=-3\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x$ and $y,$ and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$ To do this, we apply the back substitution. 

From the first equation, we get

$$
x+3z=7\,⇒\,x=7-3z
$$

and from the second equation, we obtain

$$
y+2z=-3\,⇒\,y=-3-2z.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=7-3z \\ y=-3-2z \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $z$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}7-3z \\ -3-2z \\ z\end{aligned}],\,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-38063.knowledge_point: Translating Problems With Proportional Rates of Change Into Differential Equations
q-38063.source_problem: The velocity $v$ of a merry-go-round decreases at a rate that is proportional to the velocity at that moment. What differential equation describes the rate of change of the velocity at time $t?$
q-38063.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **velocity** $v$ of a merry-go-round **decreases** at a **rate** that is **proportional** to the **velocity** at the moment.* 

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *velocity* of a merry-go-round 
varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ is *proportional to* the *velocity.* In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}∝v.
$$

Recall that $∝$ means "is proportional to."

- Finally, we want to replace the proportionality symbol with an equality symbol. Let $k$ be a positive constant. Since the velocity *decreases* with time, our derivative should be *negative*. Therefore, we can rewrite our proportionality statement as

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-kv.
$$

q-38313.knowledge_point: Further Translating Problems With Proportional Rates of Change Into Differential Equations
q-38313.source_problem:
A skater is skating straight down a ramp. The displacement $D$ of the skater increases at a rate that's proportional to the square of the time $t,$ in seconds.
What differential equation describes the rate of change of displacement $D$ at time $t,$ where $t$ is the time since he started skating?
q-38313.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*A skater is skating straight down a ramp. The **displacement** $D$ of the skater **increases** at a **rate** that's **proportional** to the **square of the time** $t,$ in seconds. *

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *displacement* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}$ is *proportional to* the *square of the time.* In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}∝{t}^{2}.
$$

Recall that $∝$ means "is proportional to."

- Finally, we want to replace the proportionality symbol with an equality symbol. Let $k$ be a positive constant. Since the displacement *increases* with time, our derivative should be *positive*. Therefore, we can rewrite our proportionality statement as

$$
\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}=k{t}^{2}.
$$

q-38324.knowledge_point: Translating Contextual Problems Into Differential Equations
q-38324.source_problem:
The size of a bush growing in a schoolyard is being monitored. The area $A\,{\text{m}}^{2}$ of the bush at any given moment grows at a rate that's directly proportional to the area at that moment. Additionally, $2\,{\text{m}}^{2}$ of the bush is cut away every month.
What is the differential equation that describes the rate of change in the area of the schoolyard bush at time $t,$ where $t$ is the time in months since it started growing?
q-38324.worked_solution:
The rate of change in the area of the bush per month increases in proportion to $A$ and decreases by $2.$ The differential equation that describes this is

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=kA-2,
$$

where $k$ is the (positive) constant of proportionality.

q-39793.knowledge_point: Calculating the Vertical Asymptotes of a Rational Function
q-39793.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)(x+1)(x-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the three solutions $x=-3,$ $x=-1$ and $x=1.$ Therefore, the equations of the vertical asymptotes are  $x=-3,\,$ $x=-1$ and $x=1.$

q-40727.knowledge_point: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral When the Limits are Given

If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the curves $y=2{x}^{2}$ and $y=1+{x}^{2},$ as shown above, then ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA=$

q-42019.knowledge_point: Solving a Consistent System of Equations Using Gauss-Jordan Elimination
q-42019.source_problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned} & x-2y+2z=2 \\  & y-z=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
q-42019.worked_solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Using the standard Gauss-Jordan method, we can reduce this matrix to reduced row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned} & x=0 \\  & y-z=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x$ and $y,$ and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=z-1 \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $z$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ z-1 \\ z\end{aligned}],\,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-42043.knowledge_point: Computing a Tangent or Cotangent Using the Pythagorean Identity
q-42043.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932638/assets/919b9e8f2a9493fd0dda3e0d7bf66de9af054fc4ed9c0fcf7a68329fdbbaffdd.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $sin⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2},$ what is the value of $tan⁡\theta ?$
q-42043.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932638/assets/948610f67267e6ec1b845d2b4e1bc4030b81a1080bcb9a44d9f974ff78c3f7b0.png)

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $cos⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $cos⁡\theta $ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$

Finally, knowing that $tan⁡\theta =\frac{sin⁡\theta }{cos⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
tan⁡\theta =\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.
$$

q-42158.knowledge_point: Reducing an Augmented Matrix for a Singular 2x2 System to REF and Solving the Resulting System
q-42158.source_problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
q-42158.worked_solution:
The system corresponding to $M$ is 

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+2y=3 \\ 0x+0y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x+2y=3.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=3-2y,$ and the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=3-2y \\ y=y\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3-2y \\ y\end{aligned}]=⟨3-2y,\,y⟩,\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-4772.knowledge_point: Calculating the Acceleration of a Particle at a Particular Moment Given Its Position
q-4772.source_problem:
The displacement (in centimeters) of an ant moving in a straight line is given by $s(t)={t}^{2}+3t,$ where $t$ is measured in seconds.
Find the ant's acceleration at $t=10$ seconds.
q-4772.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+3t) \\  & =2t+3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+3) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the acceleration at time $t=10,$ we substitute this into the above:

$$
a(10)=2\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}
$$

Therefore, the acceleration when $t=10$ seconds is $2\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

q-48254.knowledge_point: Calculating the Rate of Change of the Area Given the Rate of Change of the Side Length
q-48254.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095797/assets/a50d4de74cb016b44546791985e5e1fdc519a9b5d2d4943ff24f6d492f4fa031.png)

The sides of a square decrease in length at a rate of $2\text{ m/s}.$ At what rate is the area of the square decreasing when the sides are $10\text{ m}$ long?
q-48254.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is decreasing at a rate of $2\,\text{m/s},$ so we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-2.$ Also, when the sides are $10\,\text{m},$ we have $x=10.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =(-2)\cdot 2(10)=-40{\text{ m}}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square decreases at $40\,{\text{m}}^{2}/\text{s}.$

q-48565.knowledge_point: Differentiating a General Exponential Function Using the Chain Rule
q-48565.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f={3}^{u},\,u=2{x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}={3}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={3}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)\cdot (4x) \\  & =4x\cdot {3}^{u}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\  & =4x\cdot {3}^{2{x}^{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(3).\end{aligned}
$$

q-48860.knowledge_point: Determining the Intervals on Which a Function Is Increasing Using Differentiation
q-48860.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/61b89de34a6900d2ea39e5c2af141b3353e9ca790ac2748d0fc6d4d578127f93.png)

Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ (plotted above) is strictly increasing.
q-48860.worked_solution:
The function is strictly increasing where ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$ Differentiating $f(x)$ using the product  rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{1}{x}\cdot x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1,\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1>0.
$$

Solving $\operatorname{ln}⁡x=-1$ gives the critical point

$$
x={e}^{-1}\,⟹\,x=\frac{1}{e}.
$$

From the graph, we see that this critical point is a minimum. We also see that the slope of the tangent lines is negative to the left of the critical point and positive to the right of the critical point. 

So, we summarize the sign of the derivative in the following table:

$$
\left.\begin{aligned}x & (0,\frac{1}{e}) & \frac{1}{e} & (\frac{1}{e},\infty ) \\ f & ↘ & \text{min} & ↗ \\ {f}^{′} & - & 0 & +\end{aligned}\right|
$$

Finally, we conclude that the function is strictly increasing on the interval $(\frac{1}{e},\infty ).$

q-48909.knowledge_point: Determining Intervals of Increasing or Decreasing Displacement
q-48909.source_problem: The displacement $s,$ in meters, relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t)=(3t-5)^{2}$, where $t>0$ is the time measured in seconds. Determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x.$
q-48909.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of decreasing $x,$ then its velocity is negative. 

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((3t-5)^{2}) \\  & =6(3t-5)\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x$, we solve the inequality $v(t)<0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & <0 \\ 6(3t-5) & <0 \\ 3t-5 & <0 \\ 3t & <5 \\ t & <\frac{5}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of decreasing $x$ is $t\in (0,\frac{5}{3}).$

q-49054.knowledge_point: Finding an Equation That Determines a Minimum Distance
q-49054.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14068172/assets/47849c87c3c8cf9008b6531e740c6fc57058905cf17e31e4c93c479f337f0fbd.png)

The $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ on the curve $y={e}^{x}\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}$ that is closest to the point $(1,0)$ satisfies the equation

$$
2x-2+=0.
$$

 
What is the missing expression?
q-49054.worked_solution:
Let's consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(1,0)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x,y) & =(x-1)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y={e}^{x}\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+{y}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+{({e}^{x}\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-2+{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =0 \\ 2x-2+{e}^{2x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-51054.knowledge_point: Identifying the Reason for a Discontinuity
q-51054.source_problem:
For what reason does the function $f(x)$ below have a discontinuity at $x=-1?$ 

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+x, & x<-1 \\ {x}^{2}+1, & x\ge -1\end{aligned}
$$
q-51054.worked_solution:
Let's check the conditions necessary for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2.$

- $f(-1)=(-1)^{2}+1=2,$ so $f(-1)$ exists. $✓$

- We calculate the one-sided limits and check if they coincide:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}({x}^{3}+x) \\  & =(-1)^{3}+(-1) \\  & =-2, \\ {lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =(-1)^{2}+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the one-sided limits exist but are not equal. $\,\,\times $ $\,\,\,$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=-1$ because ${lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}f(x).$

q-51252.knowledge_point: Translating Contextual Problems Into Differential Equations
q-51252.source_problem: A tank is being filled with water. The rate of change of the volume of water in the tank $V,$ in milliliters, is directly proportional to the time $t,$ measured in hours. Additionally, the tank is also leaking $200\,\text{ml}$ of water every hour. What is the differential equation that describes the rate of change of the volume of water in the tank, at time $t,$ where $t$ is the time (in hours) since the tank started filling?
q-51252.worked_solution:
The rate of change in the volume of water in the tank per hour increases in proportion to $t$ and decreases by $200.$ The differential equation that describes this is

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=kt-200,
$$

where $k$ is the (positive) constant of proportionality.
