q-60145.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation With a Negative Leading Coefficient
q-60145.source_problem: The equation $-20{x}^{2}+60x-41=0$ can be written in the form $20(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q,$ and solve the equation.
q-60145.worked_solution:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-20{x}^{2}+60x-41) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 20{x}^{2}-60x+41 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}20{x}^{2}-60x+41 & =0 \\ 20{x}^{2}-60x & =-41 \\ 20({x}^{2}-3x) & =-41 \\ 20[{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{3}{2}x+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}] & =-41 \\ 20[{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4}] & =-41\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-20\cdot \frac{9}{4} & =-41 \\ 20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-45 & =-41 \\ 20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =45-41 \\ 20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q=4.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}20{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4 \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{4}{20} \\ {(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{5} \\ \sqrt{{(x-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{5}} \\ |x-\frac{3}{2}| & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{5}} \\ x-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ x-\frac{3}{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

q-60356.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation With a Negative Leading Coefficient
q-60356.source_problem: The equation $-3{x}^{2}-2x+6=0$ can be written in the form $3(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q-p.$
q-60356.worked_solution:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-3{x}^{2}-2x+6) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 3{x}^{2}+2x-6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+2x-6 & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}+2x & =6 \\ 3[{x}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}x] & =6 \\ 3[{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{3}x+{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}] & =6 \\ 3[{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-\frac{1}{9}] & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-3\cdot \frac{1}{9} & =6 \\ 3{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-\frac{1}{3} & =6 \\ 3{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2} & =6+\frac{1}{3} \\ 3{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2} & =\frac{19}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{1}{3}$, $q=\frac{19}{3}.$ Finally,

$$
q-p=\frac{19}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{18}{3}=6.
$$

q-60360.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation With a Positive Leading Coefficient
q-60360.source_problem: The equation $2{x}^{2}-4x-9=0$ can be written in the form $2(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q,$ and solve the equation.
q-60360.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-4x-9 & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-4x & =9 \\ 2({x}^{2}-2x) & =9 \\ 2[{x}^{2}-2\cdot 1\cdot x+{(1)}^{2}-{(1)}^{2}] & =9 \\ 2[{(x-1)}^{2}-1] & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(x-1)}^{2}-2\cdot 1 & =9 \\ 2{(x-1)}^{2}-2 & =9 \\ 2{(x-1)}^{2} & =9+2 \\ 2{(x-1)}^{2} & =11\end{aligned}
$$

So, $q=11.$

Next, we solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(x-1)}^{2} & =11 \\ {(x-1)}^{2} & =\frac{11}{2} \\ \sqrt{{(x-1)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{11}{2}} \\ |x-1| & =\sqrt{\frac{11}{2}} \\ x-1 & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{11}{2}} \\ x & =1\pm \sqrt{\frac{11}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

q-64206.knowledge_point: Solving a Second-Order Inhomogeneous ODE with Quadratic Forcing
q-64206.source_problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-12y=12{x}^{2}-32x-30
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{2x}+B{e}^{-6x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
q-64206.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta ,$ and $\gamma $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x+\beta ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=2\alpha 
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ $\beta $ and $\gamma ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
2\alpha +4(2\alpha x+\beta )-12(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma )=12{x}^{2}-32x-30
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives:

$$
-12\alpha {x}^{2}+(8\alpha -12\beta )x+(2\alpha +4\beta -12\gamma )=12{x}^{2}-32x-30
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-12\alpha =12\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ 8\alpha -12\beta =-32\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ 2\alpha +4\beta -12\gamma =-30\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-1,\beta =2,\gamma =3.$

Therefore, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-{x}^{2}+2x+3.
$$

q-64236.knowledge_point: Solving a Second-Order ODE with Exponential Forcing and Repeated Roots
q-64236.source_problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=10{e}^{x}
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x}+Bx{e}^{x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
q-64236.worked_solution:
Since the complementary function is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{x}+Bx{e}^{x},$ we have that $\lambda =1$ is the double root of the auxiliary equation.

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $10{e}^{x}.$  In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $1$, which coincides with the double root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha ({x}^{2}+2x){e}^{x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha ({x}^{2}+4x+2){e}^{x}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha ({x}^{2}+4x+2){e}^{x}-2(\alpha ({x}^{2}+2x){e}^{x})+(\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{x}) & =10{e}^{x} \\ ({x}^{2}+4x+2-2{x}^{2}-4x+{x}^{2})\alpha {e}^{x} & =10{e}^{x} \\ 2\alpha {e}^{x} & =10{e}^{x} \\ 2\alpha  & =10 \\ \alpha  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=5{x}^{2}{e}^{x}.
$$

q-64285.knowledge_point: Solving a Second-Order Inhomogeneous ODE with Affine Forcing
q-64285.source_problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-5y=-5x+6
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{5x}+B{e}^{-x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
q-64285.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha x+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=0
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$  and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
0-4\alpha -5(\alpha x+\beta )=-5x+6
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives:

$$
-5\alpha x+(-4\alpha -5\beta )=-5x+6
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-5\alpha =-5\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ -4\alpha -5\beta =6\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =1,\,\beta =-2.$

Therefore, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=x-2.
$$

q-64351.knowledge_point: Finding the Inverse Laplace Transform of a Function Using the Scalar Multiplication Property
q-64351.source_problem: Find the inverse Laplace transform for $F(s)=\frac{4s}{{s}^{2}+9}.$
q-64351.worked_solution:
From the table of Laplace transforms, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡3t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{3}^{2}}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9},\,s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by applying the inverse Laplace transform to the above result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡3t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9} \\ {L}^{-1}{L{\operatorname{cos}⁡3t}} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9}} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡3t & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9}} \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9}} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡3t.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the multiplicative property of the inverse Laplace transform, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot {L}^{-1}{\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9}}=4\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡3t \\ {L}^{-1}{\frac{4s}{{s}^{2}+9}}=4\operatorname{cos}⁡3t.\end{aligned}
$$

q-64381.knowledge_point: Finding the Inverse Laplace Transform Using Partial Fractions
q-64381.source_problem: Find the inverse Laplace transform for $F(s)=\frac{6}{{s}^{2}-6s}.$
q-64381.worked_solution:
First, we write $F(s)$ as a sum of partial fractions, as follows: 

$$
\frac{6}{{s}^{2}-6s}=\frac{6}{s(s-6)}=\frac{1}{s-6}-\frac{1}{s}
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{6t}} & =\frac{1}{s-6},\,s>6 \\ L{1} & =\frac{1}{s},\,s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the addition property of the Laplace transform, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-6}-\frac{1}{s}} & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-6}}-{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s}} \\  & ={e}^{6t}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the inverse Laplace transform of $F(s)=\frac{6}{{s}^{2}-6s}$ is $f(t)={e}^{6t}-1.$

q-64953.knowledge_point: Finding a Second Solution to a Differential Equation Using Reduction of Order
q-64953.source_problem: Given that ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}$ is a solution to the equation ${y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+y=0,$ use reduction of order to find a second solution ${y}_{2}(x)$ to the equation.
q-64953.worked_solution:
According to the reduction of order method, we let ${y}_{2}=u(x){e}^{x}.$ 

Differentiating the above with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′} & ={u}^{′}{e}^{x}+u{e}^{x}={e}^{x}({u}^{′}+u) \\ {y}_{2}^{″} & ={e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}+u).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}+u)-2{e}^{x}({u}^{′}+u)+{e}^{x}(u) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}({u}^{″}+2{u}^{′}+u-2{u}^{′}-2u+u) & =0 \\ {e}^{x}{u}^{″} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{x}\ne 0$ we must have

$$
{u}^{″}=0.
$$

Let $w={u}^{′}.$ Then our equation becomes

$$
{w}^{′}=0\,⟹\,w={c}_{1}.
$$

But since $w={u}^{′},$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}={c}_{1}\,⟹\,u={c}_{1}x+{c}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, our expression for ${y}_{2}(x)=u{e}^{x}$ becomes

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}({c}_{1}x+{c}_{2}).
$$

Finally, setting ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{x}\cdot x=x{e}^{x}.
$$

q-65130.knowledge_point: Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point
q-65130.source_problem: Given that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ evaluate ${f}_{yxx}(1,1)$ if ${f}_{xy}(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}(2+xy).$
q-65130.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yxx}(x,y) & ={f}_{xyx}(x,y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{xy}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{xy}(2+xy)) \\  & ={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}(2+xy)+{y}^{2}{e}^{xy} \\  & ={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}(3+xy).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,1):$

$$
{f}_{yxx}(1,1)=(1)^{2}{e}^{1\cdot 1}(3+(1)(1))=4e\,\,
$$

q-66435.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation With Complex Roots by Completing the Square
q-66435.source_problem: The equation ${x}^{2}+16x+164=0$ can be written in the form $(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q,$ and solve the equation.
q-66435.worked_solution:
We first move the constant to the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+16x+164 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+16x & =-164\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+16x & =-164 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 8x+{8}^{2}-{8}^{2} & =-164 \\ (x+8)^{2}-64 & =-164 \\ (x+8)^{2} & =-100\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=8,\,q=-100,$ and $p+q=-92.$

We now solve the equation using the square root method.

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+8)^{2} & =-100 \\ x+8 & =\pm \sqrt{-100} \\ x+8 & =\pm 10\,\text{i} \\ x & =-8\pm 10\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, $x=-8+10\,\text{i}$ and $x=-8-10\,\text{i}.$

q-6812.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Parametric Curve
q-6812.source_problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=({t}^{3}-1){e}^{t},\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=0.$
q-6812.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=({t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}-1){e}^{t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{({t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}-1){e}^{t}}.
$$

At the point where $t=0$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{({0}^{3}+3\cdot {0}^{2}-1){e}^{0}} \\  & =\frac{2(1)}{(-1)\cdot 1} \\  & =-2\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-70185.knowledge_point: Calculating the y-Intercepts of an Ellipse By Completing the Square
q-70185.source_problem: Determine the points where the ellipse $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-8x-4y=8$ intercepts the $y$-axis.
q-70185.worked_solution:
To calculate the $y$-intercepts, we need to substitute $x=0$ in the equation of the ellipse and try to solve the resulting equation for $y.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-8x-4y & =8 \\ 4\cdot {0}^{2}+{y}^{2}-8\cdot 0-4y & =8 \\ {y}^{2}-4y & =8 \\ (y-2)^{2}-4 & =8 \\ (y-2)^{2} & =8+4 \\ (y-2)^{2} & =12 \\ x-2 & =\pm 2\sqrt{3} \\ x & =2\pm 2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,2-2\sqrt{3})$ and $(0,2+2\sqrt{3}).$

Taking the derivative, we have

$$

$$

$$

q-71407.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient
q-71407.source_problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $z=2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x$ at the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$
q-71407.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x \\ z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(\frac{1}{2},1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)k \\  & =(-4x-1)\text{ }i-4y\text{ }j+k \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3) & =(-4(\frac{1}{2})-1)\,i-4(1)\text{ }j+k \\  & =-3\,i-4\,j+k \\  & =⟨-3,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ and passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨-3,-4,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

q-7188.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at the Moment When Its Acceleration is Zero
q-7188.source_problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=-\frac{2}{9}{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}+14t+17,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
q-7188.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{2}{9}{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}+14t+17) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{t}^{2}+6t+14\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{2}{3}{t}^{2}+6t+14) \\  & =-\frac{4}{3}t+6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-\frac{4}{3}t+6 \\ \frac{4}{3}t & =6 \\ t & =4.5\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t=4.5.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
v(4.5)=-\frac{2}{3}(4.5)^{2}+6(4.5)+14=27.5.
$$

q-7198.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
q-7198.source_problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=4-{t}^{2}$, where $t>0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
q-7198.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 4-{t}^{2} & =0 \\ (2-t)(2+t) & =0 \\ t & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t⩾0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-{t}^{2}) \\  & =-2t \\ {v}^{″}(2) & =-2(2) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(2)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (4-{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =4t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4(0)-\frac{1}{3}(0)^{3}+C & =0 \\ 0+0+C & =0\,⟹\,C=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=4t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(2)=4(2)-\frac{1}{3}(2)^{3}=\frac{16}{3}\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

q-7217.knowledge_point: Finding a Position Vector Given a Velocity Vector
q-7217.source_problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v=⟨t(3t-2),\,8{t}^{3}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(30,90)$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
q-7217.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨t(3t-2),\,8{t}^{3}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int t(3t-2)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 8{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,2{t}^{4}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨30,90⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨(3)^{3}-(3)^{2}+{C}_{1},\,2(3)^{4}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨30,90⟩ & =⟨18+{C}_{1},162+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=12$ and ${C}_{2}=-72.$ Therefore, the position vector is

$$
r(t)=⟨{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+12,\,2{t}^{4}-72⟩.
$$

q-7221.knowledge_point: Finding a Position Vector Given an Acceleration Vector
q-7221.source_problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨6t-2,4⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(0,0)$ and has velocity $⟨1,\,4⟩$ when $t=1,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
q-7221.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨6t-2,4⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (6t-2)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}-2t+{C}_{1},\,4t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(1)=⟨1,4⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨3(1)^{2}-2(1)+{C}_{1},\,4(1)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨1,4⟩ & =⟨1+{C}_{1},4+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨3{t}^{2}-2t,\,4t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3{t}^{2}-2t,\,4t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (3{t}^{2}-2t)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+{C}_{3},\,2{t}^{2}+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(1)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨(1)^{3}-(1)^{2}+{C}_{3},\,2(1)^{2}+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{3},2+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=0$ and ${C}_{4}=-2.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{3}-{t}^{2},\,2{t}^{2}-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

q-72913.knowledge_point: Calculating the x-Intercepts of an Ellipse By Completing the Square
q-72913.source_problem: Calculate the points where the ellipse $2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-20x+6y+47=0$ intercepts the $x$-axis.
q-72913.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercepts, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-20x+6y+47 & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}+3(0)^{2}-20x+6(0)+47 & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-20x+47 & =0 \\ 2[{x}^{2}-10x]+47 & =0 \\ 2[(x-5)^{2}-25]+47 & =0 \\ 2(x-5)^{2}-50+47 & =0 \\ 2(x-5)^{2} & =3 \\ (x-5)^{2} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ x-5 & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \\ x & =5\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at $(5-\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}},0)$ and $(5+\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}},0).$

q-73210.knowledge_point: Determining Intervals of Increasing or Decreasing Displacement
q-73210.source_problem: The displacement $s,$ in meters, relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t)=t{e}^{-2t}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time, measured in seconds. Find the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x.$
q-73210.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of increasing $x,$ then its velocity is positive. 

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t{e}^{-2t}) \\  & ={e}^{-2t}(1-2t)\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x$, we solve $v(t)>0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & >0 \\ {e}^{-2t}(1-2t) & >0 \\ 1-2t & >0 \\ 2t & <1 \\ t & <\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of increasing $x$ is $t\in [0,\frac{1}{2}).$

q-73397.knowledge_point: Solving a 3x3 System of Equations Using Standard Gaussian Elimination with Row Exchanges
q-73397.source_problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 5 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 & 9\end{aligned}].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form.
q-73397.worked_solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 5 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -3 & -2 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -3 & -2 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & -2 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply the $2$nd row by $-\frac{1}{3}$ and the $3$rd row by $\frac{1}{2}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & -2 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{2}{3} & -\frac{7}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{2}{3} & -\frac{7}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-73580.knowledge_point: Solving a 3x3 System of Equations Using Standard Gaussian Elimination with Row Exchanges
q-73580.source_problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}5 & 20 & -10 & -5 \\ -2 & -8 & 6 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 12\end{aligned}].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form.
q-73580.worked_solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}5 & 20 & -10 & -5 \\ -2 & -8 & 6 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ -2 & -8 & 6 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply the $2$nd row by $\frac{1}{3}$ and the $3$rd row by $\frac{1}{2}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-73617.knowledge_point: Determining the Range of a Parametric Equation
q-73617.source_problem:
Given that a curve is defined parametrically as

$$
x=1-t,\,\,\,y={t}^{2}-4,\,t\ge -1,
$$

determine the ranges of $x$ and $y.$
q-73617.worked_solution:
Let's consider each variable in turn.

- To find the range of $x,$ note that $1-t\le 2$ for all $t\ge -1.$ Consequently, $x=1-t\le 2.$

- To find the range of $y,$ note that ${t}^{2}\ge 0$ for all $t.$ Consequently, $y={t}^{2}-4\ge -4.$

Therefore, the ranges are $x\le 2$ and $y\ge -4.$

q-73740.knowledge_point: Reducing an Augmented Matrix for a Singular 2x2 System to REF and Solving the Resulting System
q-73740.source_problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ -5 & -10 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
q-73740.worked_solution:
Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ -5 & -10 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+5{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+2y=-1 \\ 0x+0y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x+2y=-1.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=-1-2y,$ and the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-1-2y \\ y=y\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1-2y \\ y\end{aligned}]\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-73999.knowledge_point: Finding the Intersection Point of a Line in Parametric Form and a Plane in Cartesian Form
q-73999.source_problem:
Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:{\begin{aligned}x=-2-t \\ y=9-3t \\ z=-1-6t\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,Π:-3x+2y+5z-85=0.
$$
q-73999.worked_solution:
We can substitute the parametric expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ of the line into the equation of the plane immediately:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+2y+5z-85 & =0 \\ -3(-2-t)+2(9-3t)+5(-1-6t) & =85 \\ 6+3t+18-6t-5-30t & =85 \\ -33t & =66 \\ t & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

To get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P$, we substitute $t=-2$ into the parametric equations of the line:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-2-(-2)=0 \\ y=9-3(-2)=15 \\ z=-1-6(-2)=11\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection point is  $P(0,15,11).$

q-74151.source_problem: Let $x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -k \\ 2k \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and $y=[\begin{aligned}k \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$ Find $k$, if the distance between the vectors is $\text{d}(x,y)=2\sqrt{3}.$
q-74151.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the distance between $x$ and $y$ in terms of $k:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}(x,y) & =‖x-y‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{y}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{y}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{y}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{y}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(3-k)^{2}+(-k-(-1))^{2}+(2k-0)^{2}+(0-(-2))^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9-6k+{k}^{2}+{k}^{2}-2k+1+4{k}^{2}+4} \\  & =\sqrt{6{k}^{2}-8k+14}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given equation  $\text{d}(x,y)=2\sqrt{3},$ we obtain an equation that we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6{k}^{2}-8k+14} & =2\sqrt{3} \\ {(\sqrt{6{k}^{2}-8k+14})}^{2} & ={(2\sqrt{3})}^{2} \\ 6{k}^{2}-8k+14 & =12 \\ 6{k}^{2}-8k+2 & =0 \\ 3{k}^{2}-4k+1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the quadratic formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}k & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-(-4)\pm \sqrt{(-4)^{2}-4(3)(1)}}{2(3)} \\  & =\frac{4\pm \sqrt{4}}{6} \\  & =\frac{4\pm 2}{6} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 1}{3},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives $k=1$ and $k=\frac{1}{3}.$

q-74626.knowledge_point: Finding the Reduced Row Echelon Form of a Singular 3x3 System With Two Pivots
q-74626.source_problem:
Consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+2y-2z=1 \\ -3x-6y+6z=-3 \\ 2x+5y=3\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
q-74626.worked_solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 1 \\ -3 & -6 & 6 & -3 \\ 2 & 5 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Transforming $M$ into reduced row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 1 \\ -3 & -6 & 6 & -3 \\ 2 & 5 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 5 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the row echelon form above, we have only two pivots (in the $1$st and $2$nd columns). To transform the matrix to reduced row echelon form, we need to create zeros above the pivots only. This gives,

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -10 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-10z=-1 \\ y+4z=1 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final equation, we can remove this equation from the system. 

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x$ and $y,$ and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=10z-1 \\ y=1-4z \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $z$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}10z-1 \\ 1-4z \\ z\end{aligned}],\,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-74628.knowledge_point: Finding the Reduced Row Echelon Form of a Singular 3x3 System With Two Pivots
q-74628.source_problem:
Consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-2z=3 \\ 7x-14z=21 \\ 2y-6z=8\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard Gauss-Jordan method to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to reduced row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
q-74628.worked_solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 7 & 0 & -14 & 21 \\ 0 & 2 & -6 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

Transforming $M$ into reduced row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 7 & 0 & -14 & 21 \\ 0 & 2 & -6 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-7){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -6 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & -6 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-2z=3 \\ y-3z=4 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any numbers $x,y,z$ form a solution of the final equation, we can remove this equation from the system. 

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variables are $x$ and $y,$ and we have one free variable, $z.$ That means we need to find $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z.$ 

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=2z+3 \\ y=3z+4 \\ z=z,\end{aligned}
$$

where $z$ (the free variable) is an arbitrary number.

In vector form, the solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2z+3 \\ 3z+4 \\ z\end{aligned}],\,z\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-75099.knowledge_point: Finding the Lower Triangular Matrix Given the Elementary Row Operations
q-75099.source_problem:
Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $H$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}.
$$

Given that $H$ has the LU factorization $H=LU,$ then $L=$
q-75099.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

q-75100.knowledge_point: Finding the Lower Triangular Matrix Given the Elementary Row Operations
q-75100.source_problem:
Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $H$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-4{R}_{1}.
$$

Given that $H$ has the LU factorization $H=LU,$ then $L=$
q-75100.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-4)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

q-75102.knowledge_point: Finding the LU Factorization Using Two or More Elementary Row Operations
q-75102.source_problem:
Given that 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$
q-75102.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ {E}_{1}A & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

q-75288.knowledge_point: Computing the Normal Line to a Parametric Curve
q-75288.source_problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={t}^{4}-3{t}^{2},\,y=2{t}^{3}-t,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=1$ on the curve. Find the equation of the normal to the curve at $C.$
q-75288.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(1)^{4}-3(1)^{2}=-2, \\ y & =2(1)^{3}-1=1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the normal at the point $(-2,1).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4{t}^{3}-6t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=6{t}^{2}-1.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{6{t}^{2}-1}{4{t}^{3}-6t}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$  the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =\frac{6(1)^{2}-1}{4(1)^{3}-6(1)} \\  & =\frac{5}{-2} \\  & =-\,\frac{5}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(\,-\frac{5}{2}\,)}=\frac{2}{5}
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-2,1)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=\frac{2}{5}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =\frac{2}{5}(x+2) \\ y & =\frac{2}{5}(x+2)+1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-75583.knowledge_point: Applying the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
q-75583.source_problem: Let $f(t)=t\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{tan}⁡t}.$ Find ${g}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ given the function $g$ is defined by $g(x)={\int }_{0}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t$ for $0<x<\frac{\pi }{2}.$
q-75583.worked_solution:
The function $f(t)=t\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{tan}⁡t}$ is continuous on $[0,x],$ where $0<x<\frac{\pi }{2}.$ So, FTC II applies, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{0}^{x}t\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{tan}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =x\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the value of ${g}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ we substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{\pi }{4}\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\sqrt[3]{1} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-7642.knowledge_point: Calculating the y-Intercepts of an Ellipse
q-7642.source_problem:
Calculate the points where the ellipse 
$\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{6}=1$ intercepts the $y$-axis.
q-7642.worked_solution:
To calculate the $y$-intercept, we need to substitute $x=0$ in the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $y.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{6} & =1 \\ \frac{(0-1)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{6} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{9}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{6} & =1 \\ 4+6(y+2)^{2} & =36 \\ 6(y+2)^{2} & =32 \\ 3(y+2)^{2} & =16 \\ (y+2)^{2} & =\frac{16}{3} \\ y+2 & =\pm \frac{4}{\sqrt{3}} \\ y & =-2\pm \frac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $y$-axis at the points $(0,-2-\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{3})$ and $(0,-2+\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}).$

q-7645.knowledge_point: Calculating the x-Intercepts of an Ellipse By Completing the Square
q-7645.source_problem: Calculate the points where the ellipse  $9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-36x+16y=-16$ intercepts the $x$-axis.
q-7645.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercepts, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-36x+16y & =-16 \\ 9{x}^{2}+4(0)^{2}-36x+16(0) & =-16 \\ 9{x}^{2}-36x & =-16 \\ {x}^{2}-4x & =-\frac{16}{9} \\ (x-2)^{2}-{2}^{2} & =-\frac{16}{9} \\ (x-2)^{2} & =-\frac{16}{9}+4 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =-\frac{16}{9}+\frac{36}{9} \\ (x-2)^{2} & =\frac{20}{9} \\ x-2 & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3} \\ x & =2\pm \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at $(2-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3},0)$ and $(2+\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3},0).$

q-7646.knowledge_point: Calculating the y-Intercepts of an Ellipse By Completing the Square
q-7646.source_problem: Determine the points where the ellipse ${x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-4x+4y=10$ intercepts the $y$-axis.
q-7646.worked_solution:
To calculate the $y$-intercepts, we need to substitute $x=0$ in the equation of the ellipse and try to solve the resulting equation for $y.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-4x+4y & =10 \\ (0)^{2}+2{y}^{2}-4(0)+4y & =10 \\ 2{y}^{2}+4y & =10 \\ {y}^{2}+2y & =5 \\ (y+1)^{2}-{1}^{2} & =5 \\ (y+1)^{2} & =5+1 \\ (y+1)^{2} & =6 \\ y+1 & =\pm \sqrt{6} \\ y & =-1\pm \sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,-1-\sqrt{6})$ and $(0,-1+\sqrt{6}).$

q-77476.knowledge_point: Determining the Dimension of the Product of Two Matrices
q-77476.source_problem:
Let
$E=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]$
and

What are the dimensions of $ER?$
q-77476.worked_solution:
We notice that $E$ is a $3\times 1$ matrix and $R$ is a $1\times 3$ matrix.

$$

$$

q-77726.knowledge_point: Computing the Image of a Point Under a Linear Transformation of a Plane
q-77726.source_problem:
Consider the linear transformation $T$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-3 & \sqrt{3} \\ 1 & \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

What are the coordinates of the point ${S}^{′}$, the image of $S(-4,\sqrt{3})$ under the action of $T?$
q-77726.worked_solution:
To find the image of $S$ under the action of $T$, we first create a column-vector $x$ containing the coordinates of $S:$

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the image of $x$ under the action of $T$ by calculating the matrix product $Tx:$

$$

$$

The result, $Tx,$ contains the coordinates of ${S}^{′}.$ Therefore, ${S}^{′}(15,-1).$

q-79306.knowledge_point: Translating Problems With Inversely Proportional Rates of Change Into Differential Equations
q-79306.source_problem: In a controlled environment, the temperature $T$ of a hot drink decreases at a rate that's inversely proportional to the cube of the temperature. What differential equation describes the rate of change of the temperature of the drink $T?$
q-79306.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*In a controlled environment, the **temperature** $T$ of a hot drink **decreases** at a rate that's **inversely proportional** to the **cube of the temperature** $T.$*

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *temperature* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}$ is *inversely proportional to* the *cube of the temperature.* In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}∝\frac{1}{{T}^{3}}.
$$

Recall that $∝$ means "is proportional to."

- Finally, we want to replace the proportionality symbol with an equality symbol. Let $k$ be a positive constant. Since the temperature *decreases* with time, our derivative should be *negative*. Therefore, we can rewrite our proportionality statement as

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{k}{{T}^{3}}.
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}$ is *proportional to* the *interval of time* since the car started moving. In other words,

$$

$$

Recall that $∝$ means "is proportional to."

- Finally, we want to replace the proportionality symbol with an equality symbol. Let $k$ be a positive constant. Since the car's displacement *increases* with time, our derivative should be *positive*. Therefore, we can rewrite our proportionality statement as

$$
\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}=kt.
$$

q-79438.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Combined Functions
q-79438.source_problem:
Given that for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t$ for $s>0.$
q-79438.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} & =L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}+L{3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} \\  & =L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}+3L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0, \\ L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4},\,s>0 \\ L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}+3L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}+3\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4}+\frac{3s}{{s}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{3s+2}{{s}^{2}+4},\,s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-79784.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order ODE Using a Substitution
q-79784.source_problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=8x{y}^{1/2}-\frac{4}{x}y\,,\,y>0.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{1/2}.$*
q-79784.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1/2}\,⟹\,y={z}^{2}\,.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{dz}{dx}=\frac{1}{2{y}^{1/2}}\frac{dy}{dx}\,⟹\,\frac{dy}{dx}=2z\frac{dz}{dx}.
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2z\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =8xz-\frac{4}{x}{z}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =4x-\frac{2}{x}z\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =4x-\frac{2}{x}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z & =4x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=4x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (4x) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =4{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z) & =4{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z)\,\text{d}x & =\int 4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ {x}^{2}z & ={x}^{4}+C \\ z & =\frac{{x}^{4}+C}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{1/2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{1/2} & =\frac{{x}^{4}+C}{{x}^{2}} \\ y & =\frac{({x}^{4}+C)^{2}}{{x}^{4}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-79847.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order Initial Value Problem Using a Substitution
q-79847.source_problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
(x+1)\frac{dy}{dx}=2{y}^{1/2}(x+1)^{3}+2y,\,y(0)=\frac{1}{4},\,x>-1.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z=(x+1)^{2}
$$

using the substitution $z={y}^{1/2}.$*
q-79847.worked_solution:
The substitution $z={y}^{1/2}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z=(x+1)^{2},
$$

with the initial condition

$$
z(0)=\sqrt{y(0)}=\frac{1}{2}\,.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=-\frac{1}{x+1},\,Q(x)=(x+1)^{2}\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\int 1/(x+1)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)^{-1}} \\  & =(x+1)^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x>-1.$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=(x+1)^{-1}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x+1}\,z) & =\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot (x+1)^{2} \\ \frac{1}{x+1}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\,z & =x+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x+1}\,z) & =x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x+1}\,z)\,\text{d}x & =\int (x+1)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{x+1}\,z & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+C \\ z & =(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+C)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we determine the value of $C$ that satisfies the initial condition $z(0)=\frac{1}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z(0) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ (0+1)(\frac{1}{2}{0}^{2}+0+C) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have 

$$
z=(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2})\,.
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by substituting the solution into $z={y}^{1/2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{1/2} & =(x+1)(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2}) \\ y & =(x+1)^{2}{(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-79945.knowledge_point: Finding a Series Solution to a Second-Order Initial Value Problem About a Non-Zero Point
q-79945.source_problem:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=\pi $, in ascending powers of $(x-\pi )$ up to and including the term in $(x-\pi )^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}={y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,y(\pi )=1,\,{y}^{′}(\pi )=-1.
$$
q-79945.worked_solution:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=\pi $:

$$
y(x)=y(\pi )+(x-\pi ){y}^{′}(\pi )+\frac{(x-\pi )^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(\pi )+\frac{(x-\pi )^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(\pi )+⋯
$$

We're given $y(\pi )$ and ${y}^{′}(\pi ),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{″}(\pi )$ and ${y}^{(3)}(\pi ).$

We substitute $y(\pi )=1$ into the given equation to find ${y}^{″}(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(\pi ) & ={y}^{2}(\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot (0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}(x)=2y{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(\pi )$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(\pi ) & =2y(\pi ){y}^{′}(\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+{y}^{2}(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =2(1)(-1)(0)+(1)^{2}(-1) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =y(\pi )+(x-\pi ){y}^{′}(\pi )+\frac{(x-\pi )^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(\pi )+\frac{(x-\pi )^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(\pi )+⋯ \\  & =1+(x-\pi )\cdot (-1)+\frac{(x-\pi )^{2}}{2}\cdot (0)+\frac{(x-\pi )^{3}}{6}\cdot (-1)+… \\  & =1-(x-\pi )-\frac{1}{6}(x-\pi )^{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

q-79950.knowledge_point: Finding a Series Solution to a First-Order Initial Value Problem
q-79950.source_problem:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=0$, in ascending powers of $x$ up to and including the term in ${x}^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=yx+{e}^{x},\,y(0)=0.
$$
q-79950.worked_solution:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=0$:

$$
y(x)=y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯
$$

We're given $y(0),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{′}(0),$  ${y}^{″}(0)$ and ${y}^{(3)}(0).$

We know that $y(0)=0,$ so we substitute this into the given equation to find ${y}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =y(0)(0)+{e}^{0}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{″}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{″}(x)={y}^{′}x+y+{e}^{x}
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{″}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(0) & ={y}^{′}(0)(0)+y(0)+{e}^{0} \\  & =0+0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

To find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate ${y}^{″}(x)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}(x)={y}^{″}x+{y}^{′}+{y}^{′}+{e}^{x}={y}^{″}x+2{y}^{′}+{e}^{x}
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(0) & ={y}^{″}(0)(0)+2{y}^{′}(0)+{e}^{0} \\  & =0+2(1)+1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯ \\  & =0+x\cdot 1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\cdot 1+\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}\cdot 3+⋯ \\  & =x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

q-79951.knowledge_point: Finding a Series Solution to a First-Order Initial Value Problem
q-79951.source_problem:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=0$, in ascending powers of $x$ up to and including the term in ${x}^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=2x-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,y(0)=-1.
$$
q-79951.worked_solution:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=0$:

$$
y(x)=y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯
$$

We're given $y(0),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{′}(0),$  ${y}^{″}(0)$ and ${y}^{(3)}(0).$

We know that $y(0)=-1,$ so we substitute this into the given equation to find ${y}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =2(0)-y(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{″}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{″}(x)=2-{y}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{″}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(0) & =2-{y}^{′}(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0+y(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =2-(1)(1)+(-1)(0) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

To find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate ${y}^{″}(x)$ with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}(x)=-{y}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-{y}^{″}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(0) & =-{y}^{″}(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0+2{y}^{′}(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡0+y(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =-(1)(1)+2(1)(0)+(-1)(1) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯ \\  & =-1+x\cdot 1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\cdot 1+\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}\cdot (-2)+⋯ \\  & =-1+x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

q-80825.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvalues of a General 3x3 Matrix
q-80825.source_problem:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}].$
q-80825.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,A-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
A-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is given by $det(A-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $1$st row, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 3 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}|-1|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-{\lambda }^{3}+6\lambda +5)-(-1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}+7\lambda +6 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}-7\lambda -6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to solve this equation. We find the first root by testing some values. According to the rational zeros theorem, a list of good first guesses consists of all divisors of $6:$ 

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 3,\pm 6
$$

- Let's pick $x=1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{3}-7(1)-6 & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =1$ is not a root of the equation.

- Let's pick $x=-1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)^{3}-7(-1)-6 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =-1$ is a root of the equation.

So, we can factor $(\lambda +1)$ out of ${\lambda }^{3}-7\lambda -6$ using synthetic division:

| $-1$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-7$ | $-6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $↓$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $6$ |
|  | $1$ | $-1$ | $-6$ | $0$ |

So, we obtain the following factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +1)({\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -6) & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=3.$

q-8171.knowledge_point: Finding the Maclaurin Expansion of a Composite Function Using a Standard Maclaurin Expansion
q-8171.source_problem: Find the first four non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of $\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{x}.$
q-8171.worked_solution:
The standard Maclaurin expansion for $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{4!}-\frac{{x}^{6}}{6!}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Replacing $x$ with $\sqrt{x}$ in the above expansion and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{x} & =1-\frac{(\sqrt{x})^{2}}{2!}+\frac{(\sqrt{x})^{4}}{4!}-\frac{(\sqrt{x})^{6}}{6!}+⋯ \\  & =1-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{24}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{720}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-8306.knowledge_point: Finding Particular Solutions of Differential Equations by First Rearranging and Then Separating
q-8306.source_problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2yx+y{x}^{2}$ that satisfies $y(1)=1.$
q-8306.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2yx+y{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(2x+{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x+{x}^{2} \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =2\int x\,\text{d}x+\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & ={x}^{2}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ y & =\pm {e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3+C} \\ y & =K{e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\pm {e}^{C}$ is an arbitrary constant. 

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)=1$ to find $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =1 \\ K{e}^{{1}^{2}+{1}^{3}/3} & =1 \\ K{e}^{4/3} & =1 \\ K & ={e}^{-4/3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2yx+y{x}^{2}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ is

$$
y={e}^{-4/3}\cdot {e}^{{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}/3}={e}^{({x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-4)/3}\,.
$$

q-83217.knowledge_point: Approximating the Value of a Function at a  Point Using Its Taylor Series
q-83217.source_problem: Use the first two non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of ${x}^{-1/2}$ about $x=9$ to approximate the value of ${8}^{-1/2}.$
q-83217.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=9.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{-1/2} \\ f(9) & ={9}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{3} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-3/2} \\ {f}^{′}(9) & =-\frac{1}{2}(9)^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{2\cdot 27}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{-1/2} & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2\cdot 27}(x-9)+⋯ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{x-9}{54}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=8$ into the above to approximate ${8}^{-1/2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{8}^{-1/2} & ≈\frac{1}{3}-\frac{8-9}{54} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{54} \\  & =\frac{19}{54}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-83429.knowledge_point: Finding the Maclaurin Expansion of a Product of Functions Using Standard Maclaurin Expansions
q-83429.source_problem: Find the first three non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of ${x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$
q-83429.worked_solution:
The standard Maclaurin expansion for $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{5!}-⋯ \\  & =x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{120}-⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

To get an expansion for ${x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ we multiply this series by ${x}^{2}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & ={x}^{2}(x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{120}-⋯) \\  & ={x}^{3}-\frac{{x}^{5}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{7}}{120}-⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-8360.knowledge_point: Writing First-Order Linear ODEs in Standard Form
q-8360.source_problem:
Write the following first-order linear ODE in standard form.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=0\,.
$$
q-8360.worked_solution:
A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Converting the given equation to standard form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y\operatorname{cot}⁡x & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{{2(\operatorname{cot}⁡x)}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}y & ={{-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the equation is written in standard form with $P(x)=2\operatorname{cot}⁡x$ and $Q(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.$

q-8369.source_problem: Which of the following is a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
q-8369.worked_solution:
A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y)
$$

is said to be homogeneous if it satisfies the following property:

$$
f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)\,
$$

The only option in which this is the case is

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

We can check this using one of two methods.

**Method 1**

Let $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}.$

We see that both the numerator and denominator are homogeneous polynomials of degree $2.$ Therefore, $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree $2-2=0.$

Hence, the original differential equation is homogeneous.

**Method 2**

To check this in detail using the definition, we first write:

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}
$$

We can check that this is homogeneous showing that $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(ty)^{2}-(tx)^{2}}{(ty)^{2}+(tx)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}{y}^{2}-{t}^{2}{x}^{2}}{{t}^{2}{y}^{2}+{t}^{2}{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2})}{{t}^{2}({y}^{2}+{x}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ the original differential equation is homogeneous.

q-85640.knowledge_point: Computing a Tangent or Cotangent Using the Pythagorean Identity
q-85640.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932638/assets/97c98411b3455c78c9e061cf54fa76eabfccc369e9e364a5366eb58bd5d2935d.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $cos⁡\theta =\frac{2}{7},$ what is the value of $cot⁡\theta ?$
q-85640.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932638/assets/8c7889d63cf5894236bc5f5e24feb64ecf5a47acb2c07c807a4e65458a991232.png)

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $sin⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $cos⁡\theta =\frac{2}{7}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{2}{7})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{4}{49}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{45}{49}} \\  & =\pm \frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $sin⁡\theta $ is negative in the fourth quadrant. So, $sin⁡\theta =-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7}.$

Finally, knowing that $cot⁡\theta =\frac{cos⁡\theta }{sin⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
cot⁡\theta =\frac{(\frac{2}{7})}{(-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7})}=-\frac{2}{3\sqrt{5}}=-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{15}.
$$

q-85643.knowledge_point: Computing a Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratio Using the Pythagorean Identity
q-85643.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932638/assets/3be6fa94deb7fc38d870e5a31cc81c3cfd6b9ab84c21340e7e88f7246b1058bc.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $y$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\frac{5}{7},$ what is the value of $sec⁡\theta ?$
q-85643.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932638/assets/17e6320115f2cf8b5ffad6abc099169774536af20d2559b453aaa97c1286d96d.png)

We're given that $y=\frac{5}{7}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, $sin⁡\theta =\frac{5}{7}.$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $cos⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{5}{7}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}cos⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{5}{7})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{25}{49}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{24}{49}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{24}}{7} \\  & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{6}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $cos⁡\theta $ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $cos⁡\theta =-\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{7}.$

Finally, knowing that $sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{cos⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
sec⁡\theta =\frac{1}{(-\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{7})}=-\frac{7}{2\sqrt{6}}=-\frac{7\sqrt{6}}{12}.
$$

q-86413.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation With a Negative Leading Coefficient
q-86413.source_problem: The equation $-4{w}^{2}-4w+11=0$ can be written in the form $4(w+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q,$ and solve the equation.
q-86413.worked_solution:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-4{w}^{2}-4w+11) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 4{w}^{2}+4w-11 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{w}^{2}+4w-11 & =0 \\ 4({w}^{2}+w) & =11 \\ 4[{w}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}w+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}] & =11 \\ 4[{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}] & =11\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{1}{4} & =11 \\ 4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-1 & =11 \\ 4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =11+1 \\ 4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q=12.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =12 \\ {(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{12}{4} \\ {(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =3 \\ \sqrt{{(w+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{3} \\ |w+\frac{1}{2}| & =\sqrt{3} \\ w+\frac{1}{2} & =\pm \sqrt{3} \\ w & =-\frac{1}{2}\pm \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

q-86414.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation With a Negative Leading Coefficient
q-86414.source_problem: The equation $-3{x}^{2}+36x-94=0$ can be written in the form $3(x+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $q-p.$
q-86414.worked_solution:
First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-3{x}^{2}+36x-94) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-36x+94 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-36x+94 & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-36x & =-94 \\ 3[{x}^{2}-12x] & =-94 \\ 3[{x}^{2}-2\cdot 6x+{6}^{2}-{6}^{2}] & =-94 \\ 3[{(x-6)}^{2}-36] & =-94\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{(x-6)}^{2}-3\cdot 36 & =-94 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2}-108 & =-94 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2} & =-94+108 \\ 3{(x-6)}^{2} & =14\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-6$, $q=14.$ Finally,

$$
q-p=14-(-6)=14+6=20.
$$

q-86758.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvalues of a General 3x3 Matrix
q-86758.source_problem:
Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$O=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].$
q-86758.worked_solution:
First, we find the matrix $\,O-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
O-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is given by $det(O-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $1$st row, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(O-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & -\lambda \end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}0 & -1-\lambda  \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-{\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}+1)+(\lambda +1) & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}+\lambda +2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to solve this equation. We find the first root by testing some values. According to the rational zeros theorem, a list of good first guesses consists of all divisors of $2:$ 

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2
$$

Let's pick $x=1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{3}+2(1)^{2}-(1)-2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =1$ is a root of the equation. So, we can factor $(\lambda -1)$ out of ${\lambda }^{3}+2{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -2$ using synthetic division:

| $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-1$ | $-2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $↓$ | $1$ | $3$ | $2$ |
|  | $1$ | $3$ | $2$ | $0$ |

So, we obtain the following factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda -1)({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +2) & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda +1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

q-87305.knowledge_point: Computing a Probability Involving Mutually Exclusive Events
q-87305.source_problem: Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events. Given that $P(B)=\frac{1}{15}$ and $P(A\cup B)=\frac{3}{5},$ find $P(A).$
q-87305.worked_solution:
If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events, then $P(A\cap B)=0.$ 

Therefore, by the addition law, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B) \\ P(A) & =P(A\cup B)-P(B) \\  & =\frac{3}{5}-\frac{1}{15} \\  & =\frac{9-1}{15} \\  & =\frac{8}{15}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-87308.knowledge_point: Computing a Probability Involving Mutually Exclusive Events
q-87308.source_problem: Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events. Given that $P(B)=\frac{18}{25}$ and $P(A\cup B)=\frac{4}{5},$ find $P(A).$
q-87308.worked_solution:
If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events, then $P(A\cap B)=0.$ 

Therefore, by the addition law, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B) & =P(A)+P(B) \\ P(A) & =P(A\cup B)-P(B) \\  & =\frac{4}{5}-\frac{18}{25} \\  & =\frac{20-18}{25} \\  & =\frac{2}{25}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-8854.knowledge_point: Solving a Second-Order ODE When the Right-Hand Side and the Complementary Solution are Dependent
q-8854.source_problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+16y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$
q-8854.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+16y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =\pm 4\text{i}$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=P\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x$ because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}=x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x)+4x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x) \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =8(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x)+16x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
8(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x)+16x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x)+16x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x)\,=4\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-8\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+8\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x=4\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡4x) \\ -8\alpha =4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡4x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{1}{2}$, $\beta =0.$
Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}=P\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡4x-\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x.
$$

q-89821.knowledge_point: Finding the Inverse Laplace Transform Using Partial Fractions
q-89821.source_problem: Find the inverse Laplace transform for $F(s)=\frac{10}{(s-2)(s+3)}.$
q-89821.worked_solution:
First, we write $F(s)$ as a sum of partial fractions, as follows: 

$$
\frac{10}{(s-2)(s+3)}=\frac{2}{s-2}-\frac{2}{s+3}
$$

From the table of Laplace transforms, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{2t}} & =\frac{1}{s-2},\,s>2 \\ L{{e}^{-3t}} & =\frac{1}{s+3},\,s>-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the addition property of the Laplace transform, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}{\frac{2}{s-2}-\frac{2}{s+3}} & =2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-2}}-2{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s+3}} \\  & =2{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{-3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the inverse Laplace transform of $F(s)=\frac{10}{(s-2)(s+3)}$ is $f(t)=2{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{-3t}.$

q-90054.knowledge_point: Working With Systems Containing Inequalities Presented in Standard Form
q-90054.source_problem:
