Which of the following systems of inequalities defines the shaded region shown above?
q-90054.worked_solution:
Consider the line $x+y=3.$ Since the line is dashed, the inequality is strict. Writing the equation of this line in slope-intercept form, we have

$$
y=-x+3.
$$

Now, since the shaded region lies *above* the line, the inequality is a "greater than"  inequality. So the corresponding inequality is

$$
y>-x+3,
$$

    

which we can rewrite as

$$
x+y>3.
$$

Now consider the line $y=2x.$ Since the line is dashed, the inequality is strict.  Also, since the shaded region lies *above* the line, the inequality is a "greater than" inequality. So the corresponding inequality is

$$
y>2x.
$$

Therefore, the system of inequalities that defines the shaded region is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+y>3 \\ y>2x.\end{aligned}
$$

q-90725.knowledge_point: Identifying Non-Solutions of Second-Order Homogeneous ODEs
q-90725.source_problem: Given that $y=y(x)$ satisfies the equation ${y}^{″}+8{y}^{′}+15y=0,$ which of the following **cannot** be $y(x)?$
q-90725.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+8\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+15{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +15) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda +15 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
(\lambda +3)(\lambda +5)=0,
$$

and so the solutions of the auxiliary equation  are $\lambda =-3$ or $\lambda =-5.$

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{-3x}$ and ${e}^{-5x}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only ${e}^{5x}$ is not a solution.

q-93675.knowledge_point: Solving a Second-Order ODE with Exponential Forcing
q-93675.source_problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+8y=12{e}^{-2x}
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)={e}^{-2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x),$ find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
q-93675.worked_solution:
Since the complementary function is ${y}_{c}(x)={e}^{-2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x),$ the roots of the auxiliary equation are $\lambda =-2\pm 2\text{i}.$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $12{e}^{-2x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $-2$, which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{-2x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=-2\alpha {e}^{-2x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=4\alpha {e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\alpha {e}^{-2x}+4(-2\alpha {e}^{-2x})+8(\alpha {e}^{-2x}) & =12{e}^{-2x} \\ (4-8+8)\alpha {e}^{-2x} & =12{e}^{-2x} \\ 4\alpha {e}^{-2x} & =12{e}^{-2x} \\ \alpha  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=3{e}^{-2x}.
$$

q-93678.knowledge_point: Solving a Second-Order ODE When the Right-Hand Side and the Complementary Solution are Linearly Dependent
q-93678.source_problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4y=10{e}^{-x}
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{4x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
q-93678.worked_solution:
Since the complementary function is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{4x},$ the roots of the auxiliary equation are $\lambda =-1$ and $\lambda =4.$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $10{e}^{-x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $-1$, which coincides with one of the roots of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{-x}.
$$

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (1-x){e}^{-x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (x-2){e}^{-x}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (x-2){e}^{-x}-3(\alpha (1-x){e}^{-x})-4(\alpha x{e}^{-x}) & =10{e}^{-x} \\ (x-2-3+3x-4x)\alpha {e}^{-x} & =10{e}^{-x} \\ -5\alpha {e}^{-x} & =10{e}^{-x} \\ -5\alpha  & =10 \\ \alpha  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-2x{e}^{-x}.
$$

q-93686.knowledge_point: Solving a Second-Order ODE with Exponential Forcing and Repeated Roots
q-93686.source_problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+6\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+9y=6{e}^{-3x}
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-3x}+Bx{e}^{-3x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
q-93686.worked_solution:
Since the complementary function is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-3x}+Bx{e}^{-3x},$ we have that $\lambda =-3$ is the double root of the auxiliary equation.

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $6{e}^{-3x}.$  In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $-3$, which coincides with the double root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{-3x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (2x-3{x}^{2}){e}^{-3x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (9{x}^{2}-12x+2){e}^{-3x}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (9{x}^{2}-12x+2){e}^{-3x}+6(\alpha (2x-3{x}^{2}){e}^{-3x})+9(\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{-3x}) & =6{e}^{-3x} \\ (9{x}^{2}-12x+2+12x-18{x}^{2}+9{x}^{2})\alpha {e}^{-3x} & =6{e}^{-3x} \\ 2\alpha {e}^{-3x} & =6{e}^{-3x} \\ 2\alpha  & =6 \\ \alpha  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=3{x}^{2}{e}^{-3x}.
$$

q-93687.knowledge_point: Solving a Second-Order ODE with Exponential Forcing and Repeated Roots
q-93687.source_problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+10\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+25y=4{e}^{-5x}
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-5x}+Bx{e}^{-5x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
q-93687.worked_solution:
Since the complementary function is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-5x}+Bx{e}^{-5x},$ we have that $\lambda =-5$ is the double root of the auxiliary equation.

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $4{e}^{-5x}.$  In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $-5$, which coincides with the double root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{-5x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha (2x-5{x}^{2}){e}^{-5x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\alpha (25{x}^{2}-20x+2){e}^{-5x}.
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha (25{x}^{2}-20x+2){e}^{-5x}+10(\alpha (2x-5{x}^{2}){e}^{-5x})+25(\alpha {x}^{2}{e}^{-5x}) & =4{e}^{-5x} \\ (25{x}^{2}-20x+2+20x-50{x}^{2}+25{x}^{2})\alpha {e}^{-5x} & =4{e}^{-5x} \\ 2\alpha {e}^{-5x} & =4{e}^{-5x} \\ 2\alpha  & =4 \\ \alpha  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=2{x}^{2}{e}^{-5x}.
$$

q-93785.knowledge_point: Solving a Second-Order Inhomogeneous ODE with Affine Forcing
q-93785.source_problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=3x+4
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
q-93785.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha x+\beta 
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=0
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$  and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
0+2\alpha +(\alpha x+\beta )=3x+4
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives:

$$
\alpha x+(2\alpha +\beta )=3x+4
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\alpha =3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ 2\alpha +\beta =4\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =3,\,\beta =-2.$

Therefore, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=3x-2.
$$

q-93824.knowledge_point: Solving a Second-Order ODE When the Right-Hand Side and the Complementary Solution are Dependent
q-93824.source_problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+36y=-12\operatorname{cos}⁡6x
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡6x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡6x,$ find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
q-93824.worked_solution:
The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x$ because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x)+6x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡6x) \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =12(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡6x)-36x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x)\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
12(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡6x)-36x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x)+36x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡6x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡6x)=-12\operatorname{cos}⁡6x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-12\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡6x+12\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡6x=-12\operatorname{cos}⁡6x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}12\beta =-12\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡6x) \\ -12\alpha =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡6x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =0$ and $\beta =-1.$ Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡6x.
$$

q-93827.knowledge_point: Solving a Second-Order Inhomogeneous ODE with Quadratic Forcing
q-93827.source_problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y=-2{x}^{2}-4x+3
$$

has the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-2x}+Bx{e}^{-2x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.
q-93827.worked_solution:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta ,$ and $\gamma $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x+\beta ,\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=2\alpha 
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ $\beta $ and $\gamma ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
2\alpha +4(2\alpha x+\beta )+4(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma )=-2{x}^{2}-4x+3
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives:

$$
4\alpha {x}^{2}+(8\alpha +4\beta )x+(2\alpha +4\beta +4\gamma )=-2{x}^{2}-4x+3
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}4\alpha =-2\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ 8\alpha +4\beta =-4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ 2\alpha +4\beta +4\gamma =3\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{1}{2},\beta =0,\gamma =1.$

Therefore, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+1.
$$

q-94304.knowledge_point: Calculating the Position of a Particle Oscillating With Forced Harmonic Motion at a Moment
q-94304.source_problem:
The position $y(t),$ measured in centimeters, of a particle oscillating with forced harmonic motion without damping is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+49y=-24\operatorname{cos}⁡t,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the particle is initially at the origin with zero velocity, find the position of the particle after $\frac{\pi }{2}$ seconds.
q-94304.worked_solution:
The general solution to the equation of forced harmonic motion without damping is the sum of the complementary function and a particular solution.

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ represents simple harmonic motion and can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=49\,⟹\,\omega =7.
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡7t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡7t.
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t).$

The external force is $-24\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular integral is

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡t+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡t,
$$

where $\alpha ,\beta $ are constants to be determined.

Substituting ${y}_{p}$ into the differential equation and equating coefficients gives $\alpha =-\frac{1}{2},\beta =0.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡7t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡7t-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

Since the particle is initially at the origin with zero velocity, the initial conditions are $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$

Solving with these conditions for $A$ and $B$ gives

$$
A=\frac{1}{2},\,B=0.
$$

So our solution is

$$
y(t)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡7t-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

To find the position of the particle after $\frac{\pi }{2}$ seconds, we substitute into the equation $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{2})-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=0\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-9461.knowledge_point: Calculating the x-Intercepts of an Ellipse By Completing the Square
q-9461.source_problem: Calculate the points where the ellipse ${x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}+6x+6y=3$  intercepts the $x$-axis.
q-9461.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercepts, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}+6x+6y & =3 \\ {x}^{2}+3\cdot {0}^{2}+6x+6\cdot 0 & =3 \\ {x}^{2}+6x & =3 \\ (x+3)^{2}-9 & =3 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =3+9 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =12 \\ x+3 & =\pm 2\sqrt{3} \\ x & =-3\pm 2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at $(-3-2\sqrt{3},0)$ and $(-3+2\sqrt{3},0).$

q-9472.knowledge_point: Calculating the y-Intercepts of an Ellipse By Completing the Square
q-9472.source_problem: Determine the points where the ellipse $3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6\sqrt{3}x-6y+6=0$ intercepts the $y$-axis.
q-9472.worked_solution:
To calculate the $y$-intercepts, we need to substitute $x=0$ in the equation of the ellipse and try to solve the resulting equation for $y.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6\sqrt{3}x-6y+6 & =0 \\ 3(0)^{2}+{y}^{2}-6\sqrt{3}(0)-6y+6 & =0 \\ {y}^{2}-6y+6 & =0 \\ (y-3)^{2}-9+6 & =0 \\ (y-3)^{2} & =3 \\ y-3 & =\pm \sqrt{3} \\ y & =3\pm \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,3-\sqrt{3})$ and $(0,3+\sqrt{3}).$

q-94981.knowledge_point: Finding the Singular Values of a Square Matrix
q-94981.source_problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}]?$
q-94981.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 \\ -2 & -4 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4-\lambda  & -4 \\ -2 & -4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & -4 \\ -4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}0 & 4-\lambda  \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )((4-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16)-4(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(20-4\lambda -5\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-16)-4(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +4)-4(4-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +4-4) & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -4)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,4,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

q-95337.knowledge_point: Finding the Singular Values of a Square Matrix
q-95337.source_problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]?$
q-95337.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}0 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \,\,-1 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 0 & \,\,-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & 2-\lambda  \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(2-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-(2-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-1) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda ) & =0 \\ \lambda (2-\lambda )^{2} & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,2,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

q-95354.knowledge_point: Finding the Singular Values of a Rectangular Matrix
q-95354.source_problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]?$
q-95354.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1-\lambda  & 0\end{aligned}|+(1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ -(1-\lambda )+(1-\lambda )[(2-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-1)] & =0 \\ -(1-\lambda )+(1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +1-1) & =0 \\ \lambda (1-\lambda )(\lambda -3) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{3} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

q-95377.knowledge_point: Finding the Singular Values of a Rectangular Matrix
q-95377.source_problem: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}]?$
q-95377.worked_solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -2 & \,\,-2 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 8 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )[(8-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-4)]+2(-2)(1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +4)+(-4)(1-\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda +4-4) & =0 \\ \lambda (1-\lambda )(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{9}=3 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}
$$

q-95740.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine
q-95740.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $25{x}^{2}=(5x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{e}^{\pi }}{\sqrt{25{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{{e}^{\pi }}{\sqrt{(5x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{\pi }\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{5}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{5}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡5x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-98116.knowledge_point: Finding an Equation Implied by the Mean Value Theorem
q-98116.source_problem: Let $f(x,y)$ be a function that is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where $a=⟨1,2⟩$ and $b=⟨2,3⟩$ are the position vectors of $A$ and $B,$ respectively. If $f(a)=1$ and $f(b)=6,$ then according to the mean value theorem, which of the following must be true for some point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c?$
q-98116.worked_solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(b)-f(a) & =∇f(c)·(b-a) \\ 6-1 & =⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c)⟩\cdot (⟨2,3⟩-⟨1,2⟩) \\ 5 & =⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c)⟩\cdot ⟨1,1⟩ \\ 5 & ={f}_{x}(c)+{f}_{y}(c).\end{aligned}
$$

q-98553.knowledge_point: Finding the Best Linear Approximation of a Multivariable Function
q-98553.source_problem: Let $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2).$
q-98553.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot ⟨x+1,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & ={e}^{y}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=2, \\ {f}_{y} & =x{e}^{y} &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)=-1{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =⟨2,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)+∇\,f(-1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\  & =-2+⟨2,-2⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,\,y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2⟩ \\  & =-2+2(x+1)-2(y-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+2x-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

q-98554.knowledge_point: Finding the Best Linear Approximation of a Multivariable Function
q-98554.source_problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡z.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1,e).$
q-98554.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1,e)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,1,e)+∇f(1,1,e)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1,z-e⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(1,1,e)=0.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =y\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(1,1,e)=1, \\ {f}_{y} & =x\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(1,1,e)=1, \\ {f}_{z} & =-\frac{1}{z}\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{z}(1,1,e)=-\frac{1}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(1,1,e)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(1,1,e) & =⟨1,1,-\frac{1}{e}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,1,e)+∇f(1,1,e)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1,z-e⟩ \\  & =0+⟨1,1,-\frac{1}{e}⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1,z-e⟩ \\  & =0+1(x-1)+1(y-1)-\frac{1}{e}(z-e) \\  & =-1+x+y-\frac{z}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-98555.knowledge_point: Finding the Best Linear Approximation of a Multivariable Function
q-98555.source_problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=\frac{9}{x+2y-z}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,1,1).$
q-98555.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,1,1)+∇f(2,1,1)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-1,z-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(2,1,1)=3.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =-\frac{9}{(x+2y-z)^{2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(2,1,1)=-\frac{9}{(2+2(1)-1)^{2}}=-1, \\ {f}_{y} & =-\frac{18}{(x+2y-z)^{2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(2,1,1)=-\frac{18}{(2+2(1)-1)^{2}}=-2, \\ {f}_{z} & =\frac{9}{(x+2y-z)^{2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(2,1,1)=\frac{9}{(2+2(1)-1)^{2}}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(2,1,1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(2,1,1) & =⟨{f}_{x}(2,1,1),{f}_{y}(2,1,1),{f}_{z}(2,1,1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,1,1)+∇f(2,1,1)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-1,z-1⟩ \\  & =3+⟨-1,-2,1⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y-1,z-1⟩ \\  & =3-1(x-2)-2(y-1)+1(z-1) \\  & =6-x-2y+z.\end{aligned}
$$

q-9926.knowledge_point: Finding the Interval of Convergence of a Given Power Series
q-9926.worked_solution:
To apply the ratio test we define ${a}_{n}=\frac{{x}^{n}}{{n}^{3/2}}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{x}^{n+1}}{(n+1)^{3/2}}\cdot \frac{{n}^{3/2}}{{x}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{n}{n+1})}^{3/2}|x| \\  & =|x|{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{n}{n+1})}^{3/2} \\  & =|x|\cdot 1 \\  & =|x|\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied for $|x|<1.$ So, the radius of convergence is $1,$ and the series converges for any $x$ that lies in the open interval $(-1,1).$

The ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series when $L=1.$ So, when $|x|=1,$ we do not know if the series converges. This means that the endpoints $x=-1$ and $x=1$ need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.

- When $x=1$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{{n}^{3/2}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{1}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{2}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{3}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{4}^{3/2}}+⋯\,,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the $p$-series test.  So the endpoint $x=1$ is included in our interval.

- When $x=-1$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{{n}^{3/2}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3/2}} \\  & =-\,\frac{1}{{1}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{2}^{3/2}}-\frac{1}{{3}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{4}^{3/2}}+⋯\,,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the alternating series test.  So the endpoint $x=-1$ is included in our interval.

Therefore, the interval of convergence is $[-1,1].$
